newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts see no cut in Swedish repo rate next week.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see no cut in Swedish repo rate next week.

text.p: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, will not cut its key repurchase rate next Tuesday, according to 10 analysts polled by Reuters on Friday.
The analysts said there has not been much further information for the Riksbank to act on since it last cut the repo rate to 4.10 percent from 4.35 percent on December 17.
"I think the Riksbank will wait for CPI figures for December before cutting further," Katharina Hoyland, economist at JP Morgan, told Reuters.
"When these (statistics) have been released, I think the Riksbank will cut the repo rate by 25 basis points."
National statistics agency SCB will release December CPI data on January 21.
Danish banking group Unibank said on Friday that it expected the next cut in the repo at the end of January at the earliest.
"But the persistent weakening of the crown is an uncertainty factor," the bank said in a statement.
On Friday, Stockholm traders said the Riksbank was probably selling marks to support the crown, which was trading at 4.4415 crowns to a mark, up from 4.4160 late on Thursday.

Stockholm brokerage Hagstromer & Qviberg, which also does not expect a repo rate cut on Tuesday, said on Friday that the Riksbank could cut the repo rate to a level below 3.50 percent in a few months time.
"Why would, for example, 3.50 percent be a suitable level, when all comparable EU countries have key rates of between 3.00 and 3.15 percent?" Hagstromer & Qviberg said in a statement.
At the moment, the lowest forecast for the repo rate bottom is 3.50 percent but Hagstromer & Qviberg said it could very well fall below that level.
One reason for a repo below 3.50 percent is that the Riksbank has not managed to reach its target of keeping inflation at two percent with an allowed deviation of one percentage point on either side.
In November, annual inflation was negative at 0.3 percent.
For most of 1996 the repo rate was cut every second week, taking it down from a level of 8.91 percent early in the year in a low inflation climate.
The ten firms included in the poll were Aragon, Hagstromer & Qviberg, HSBC Midland, J P Morgan, Lehman Brothers, Nomura Bank, PaineWebber, S-E-Banken, Swedbank and Unibank Markets.
